choices: Applicants may either apply online or a visit to the office.
Applicants may either apply online or visiting the office.
Applicants either may apply online or they can visit the office.
Applicants may either apply online or visit the office.
answer: Applicants may either apply online or visit the office.
hints: "Either … or" joins two options. The two options should be in the same form.
In each choice, look at the words right after "either" and right after "or".
If "either" is followed by a plain action word (like "apply"), "or" must be followed by the same kind of word. Check each choice.

solution.methodName: Line up the parts, then match the forms

steps.action: In each choice, find what follows "either" and what follows "or".
First choice: "apply online" (an action) against "a visit to the office" (a thing). They do not match. Wrong.
Second choice: "apply online" against "visiting the office" (an -ing form). They do not match. Wrong.
Third choice: "may apply online" against "they can visit the office". The second half has its own subject, "they", but the first does not. Wrong.
steps.why: "Either" sits before "may", so the first option starts with a verb, while the second option starts with a subject.

steps.action: Fourth choice: "apply online" against "visit the office". Both are plain action words, so they match. Correct.
The answer is "Applicants may either apply online or visit the office."

trapNotes.Applicants may either apply online or a: "A visit" and "visit" look alike, but "a visit" is a thing (a noun), while "apply" is an action.
trapNotes.Applicants may either apply online or vi: "Visiting" is an -ing form, but "apply" is a plain verb. Use the same form for both: "apply … or visit".
trapNotes.Applicants either may apply online or th: It sounds natural in speech, but the half after "or" adds a new subject, "they", so the two halves do not match.
